description_full: Dauch Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, designs, engineers, and manufactures driveline and metal forming technologies that supports electric, hybrid, and internal combustion vehicles. It operates through two segments, Driveline and Metal Forming segments. The Driveline segment offers front and rear axles, driveshafts, differential assemblies, clutch modules, balance shaft systems, disconnecting driveline technology, and electric and hybrid driveline products and systems for light trucks, sport utility vehicles, crossover vehicles, passenger cars, and commercial vehicles. The Metal Forming segment provides range of products, such as engine, transmission, driveline, and safety-critical components for traditional internal combustion engine and electric vehicle architectures, including light vehicles, commercial vehicles, and off-highway vehicles, as well as products for industrial markets. It operates in North America, Asia, Europe, and South America. Dauch Corporation was formerly known as American Axle & Manufacturing Holdings, Inc. and changed its name to Dauch Corporation in January 2026. The company was founded in 1994 and is headquartered in Detroit, Michigan.

financial_summary: Dauch Corporation is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $1.1B market cap on $5.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +0% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 5% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 14% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.
The business throws off $155M in free cash flow — roughly 3 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.9× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 0.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 0.3%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 2.6% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
